content: Haemophilus is a genus of bacteria that are Gram-negative, pleomorphic, and typically appear as coccobacilli. Although they are generally small coccobacilli, they are classified as pleomorphic because they can occasionally exhibit a wide variety of shapes. This genus includes both commensal organisms and significant pathogenic strains. Notable pathogenic species include Haemophilus influenzae, which can cause sepsis and bacterial meningitis in young children, and Haemophilus ducreyi, the causative agent of chancroid. All members of the Haemophilus genus are either aerobic or facultatively anaerobic. Haemophilus species are classified based on the characteristics of their capsule, with seven serogroups identified: a through f, and e′. Among these, capsule type b (Hib) is the most clinically significant due to its high virulence. Metabolism Members of the Haemophilus genus are typically cultured on blood agar plates because they require at least one of two blood-derived growth factors: hemin (also known as factor X) and/or nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD, also known as factor V). Chocolate agar is an excellent medium for growing Haemophilus species because it enhances the availability of these essential growth factors. Alternatively, Haemophilus can be cultured using the Staph streak technique. In this method, both Staphylococcus and Haemophilus organisms are cultured together on a single blood agar plate. In such cases, Haemophilus colonies often grow as small satellite colonies around the larger Staphylococcus colonies. This occurs because the metabolic activity of Staphylococcus produces the necessary blood factor by-products required for Haemophilus growth.
